corpusNote: Aristotle's surviving corpus is a paradox: what we read are his 'esoteric' works — lecture courses, research notes, and treatises for use inside the Lyceum, never polished for publication — while the 'exoteric' works he actually published, the dialogues Cicero praised for a 'golden river' of eloquence, are entirely lost. The extant treatises reach us not through continuous copying but through a dramatic transmission: on the standard ancient story (Strabo, Plutarch) the library passed to Theophrastus, then to Neleus, then mouldered in a cellar at Skepsis until the 1st century BCE, when Andronicus of Rhodes edited and arranged them into the corpus and roughly the order we still use. Every citation is by Bekker number, from the 1831 Berlin edition.

referenceSystems.name: Bekker numbering
referenceSystems.note: The universal citation system, from Immanuel Bekker's Prussian Academy edition (Berlin 1831): page, column (a/b), line — e.g. Metaphysics 1025a. Continuous across the whole corpus, so a Bekker number alone identifies the passage.

referenceSystems.name: Ross Oxford edition
referenceSystems.note: W.D. Ross (ed.), the Oxford Classical Texts and the Oxford translation series (The Works of Aristotle Translated into English, 12 vols., 1908–1952), the basis of the Revised Oxford Translation (Barnes, ed., 1984).

referenceSystems.name: Rose fragments
referenceSystems.note: V. Rose, Aristotelis qui ferebantur librorum fragmenta (3rd ed., 1886) — the standard numbering for the fragments of the lost works. Also Gigon (1987) and, for the Constitutions, the separate collections.

works.title: Categories
works.extent: Complete. Bekker 1a–15b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; the most-commented single text of antiquity (Porphyry's Isagoge was written as its introduction), central to the medieval logic curriculum.
works.authenticity: Genuine, though the final section (the 'Postpraedicamenta', 11b–15b) is sometimes doubted as an appendix.
works.summary: The ten categories — the highest kinds of predication: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, affection. Primary substances (this man, this horse) as the ultimate subjects; secondary substances (species and genera). The foundation of the whole Western analysis of predication and being.
editions: Minio-Paluello, OCT Categoriae et Liber de Interpretatione (1949)
translations: Ackrill, Aristotle's Categories and De Interpretatione (Clarendon, 1963); Barnes (ed.), Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: On Interpretation (De Interpretatione)
works.extent: Complete. Bekker 16a–24b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: On statements (propositions): nouns, verbs, affirmation and negation, contradiction, the square of opposition, modality — and in chapter 9 the famous problem of future contingents (the sea-battle tomorrow) and its threat to bivalence and determinism.
editions: Minio-Paluello, OCT (1949)
translations: Ackrill (Clarendon, 1963); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Prior Analytics
works.extent: Complete, 2 books. Bekker 24a–70b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: The syllogistic — the first formal logic: the theory of the categorical syllogism, its figures and moods, conversion, and modal syllogistic. The founding work of formal logic, unsurpassed until the 19th century.
editions: Ross, Aristotle's Prior and Posterior Analytics (1949); Striker, Clarendon (Bk I, 2009)
translations: Smith, Aristotle: Prior Analytics (1989); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Posterior Analytics
works.extent: Complete, 2 books. Bekker 71a–100b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: Aristotle's theory of scientific knowledge (epistēmē) and demonstration (apodeixis): knowledge as grasp of the cause, the structure of a demonstrative science from first principles, definition, and — in the celebrated final chapter (II.19) — how the first principles themselves are grasped, through induction and nous (intuitive understanding). The philosophy of science of the ancient world.
editions: Ross (1949); Barnes, Clarendon (2nd ed. 1993)
translations: Barnes, Aristotle: Posterior Analytics (Clarendon, 1975; 2nd ed. 1993)

works.title: Topics
works.extent: Complete, 8 books. Bekker 100a–164b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine; among the earliest of the logical works.
works.summary: The art of dialectical reasoning from reputable opinions (endoxa): the 'topics' (topoi) or argument-schemes for constructing and refuting arguments in debate, the four predicables (definition, genus, property, accident), and dialectic as method. The practical companion to the demonstrative logic of the Analytics.
editions: Ross, Aristotelis Topica et Sophistici Elenchi (OCT, 1958)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Smith, Clarendon (Bks I & VIII, 1997)

works.title: Sophistical Refutations
works.extent: Complete (often counted as Topics Book IX). Bekker 164a–184b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: A taxonomy of fallacies — the ways arguments deceive, both those depending on language (equivocation, amphiboly, composition/division, accent, form of expression) and those independent of it (accident, secundum quid, ignoratio elenchi, begging the question, false cause, many questions). The founding work on fallacy; its closing note claims logic as an entirely new invention with no predecessors.
editions: Ross, OCT (1958)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Physics
works.extent: Complete, 8 books. Bekker 184a–267b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; Simplicius' and Philoponus' vast commentaries preserve much else (incl. Presocratic fragments).
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: The principles of nature and change: the four causes (material, formal, efficient, final); matter and form; the analysis of motion (kinēsis); place, void (denied), time as 'the number of motion'; the infinite; and in Book VIII the argument for a first unmoved mover of the eternal cosmic motion. The foundation of two millennia of physics.
editions: Ross, Aristotle's Physics (1936, with commentary); OCT
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Waterfield/Bostock (Oxford World's Classics, 1996)

works.title: On the Heavens (De Caelo)
works.extent: Complete, 4 books. Bekker 268a–313b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: The structure of the cosmos: the fifth element (aether) of the eternal heavens, moving in perfect circles; the finite, spherical, geocentric universe; the natural motions and places of the four sublunary elements; the eternity and uniqueness of the world. The physical cosmology that Ptolemaic astronomy and medieval Christendom inherited.
editions: Allan, Aristotelis De Caelo (OCT, 1936)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Leggatt (1995)

works.title: On Generation and Corruption (De Generatione et Corruptione)
works.extent: Complete, 2 books. Bekker 314a–338b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: Coming-to-be and passing-away as distinct from other change; mixture (mixis); the four elements and their transformation through the four primary qualities (hot/cold, wet/dry); the role of the sun's cycle in sustaining the eternal round of generation. Aristotle's chemistry.
editions: Joachim (1922); Rashed, Budé (2005)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Williams, Clarendon (1982)

works.title: Meteorology (Meteorologica)
works.extent: Complete, 4 books (Book IV's authenticity sometimes questioned). Bekker 338a–390b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine; Book IV (on the 'chemistry' of homogeneous bodies) is occasionally doubted or assigned to Strato.
works.summary: Phenomena of the sublunary region 'aloft': comets, the Milky Way (wrongly placed below the moon), rain, hail, winds, rivers, the sea, earthquakes, thunder and lightning, rainbows and haloes. Aristotle's earth science.
editions: Fobes (1919); Louis, Budé (1982)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: On the Soul (De Anima)
works.extent: Complete, 3 books. Bekker 402a–435b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; the subject of major commentaries by Alexander, Themistius, Philoponus, and (mediating to the West) Averroes.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: The soul as the form/first actuality of a living body — hylomorphic, not a separate substance: the nutritive, perceptive, and rational capacities; the analysis of the five senses and the 'common sense'; imagination (phantasia); and in III.5 the notoriously compressed doctrine of the 'active intellect' (nous poiētikos), the one part said to be 'separable, impassive, unmixed' and immortal — the most disputed passage in Aristotle. Foundational for philosophy of mind and biology alike.
editions: Ross, Aristotle: De Anima (1961); Jannone/Barbotin, Budé (1966)
translations: Hamlyn, Clarendon (1968; 2nd ed. 1993); Shields, Clarendon (2016)

works.title: Parva Naturalia (the short natural treatises)
works.extent: A group of seven (or nine) short works. Bekker 436a–486a.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus, transmitted and commented as a set.
works.authenticity: Genuine (De Spiritu, sometimes appended, is spurious).
works.summary: Studies of functions common to soul and body: Sense and Sensibilia (De Sensu); On Memory and Recollection; On Sleep and Waking; On Dreams; On Divination in Sleep; On Length and Shortness of Life; On Youth and Old Age, Life and Death, and Respiration. The bridge between the De Anima and the biological works.
editions: Ross, Aristotle: Parva Naturalia (1955)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Clarendon volumes (Sorabji on Memory, 1972)

works.title: The biological works (History, Parts, Generation, Movement, Progression of Animals)

date.note: Partly the fruit of Aristotle's years on Lesbos studying marine life.

works.extent: Five treatises totalling the largest bloc of the corpus — roughly a quarter of all Aristotle. History of Animals (10 bks, Bekker 486a–638b), Parts of Animals (4 bks, 639a–697b), Movement of Animals (698a–704b), Progression of Animals (704a–714b), Generation of Animals (5 bks, 715a–789b).
works.transmission: Andronican corpus. Neglected for centuries, they were vindicated by Darwin, who wrote that Linnaeus and Cuvier were 'mere schoolboys to old Aristotle'.
works.authenticity: Genuine (History of Animals Bks VII, IX, X are partly doubted).
works.summary: The foundation of biology: the systematic description (History) and causal explanation (Parts, Generation) of animal life; the four causes applied to organisms, with the primacy of the final cause (function); the classification of animals; embryology and the theory of reproduction (form from the male, matter from the female); the mechanics of animal motion. Aristotle the working scientist.
editions: Louis, Budé editions; Balme, History of Animals VII–X (Loeb, 1991); Peck, Loeb editions
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Clarendon Aristotle (Lennox on Parts of Animals, 2001)

works.title: Metaphysics

date.note: A compilation of separately composed treatises, assembled — and given the accidental title 'after the Physics' — by Andronicus, not Aristotle.

works.extent: 14 books (lettered A, α, B, Γ, Δ, E, Z, H, Θ, I, K, Λ, M, N). Bekker 980a–1093b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; not a unified work but the editor's collection of pragmateiai on being. Book α is a later addition; Book K partly duplicates B, Γ, E and Physics.
works.authenticity: Genuine, but composite. The title itself is an artefact of the edition — 'metaphysics' as a name for the discipline is a byproduct of Andronicus' shelving.
works.summary: The science of 'being qua being': the four causes and the history of earlier philosophy (A); the aporiai (B); the defence of the principle of non-contradiction (Γ); the philosophical lexicon (Δ); the central books on substance (ousia), essence, form, matter, and actuality/potentiality (Z, H, Θ) — the hardest and most important stretch; unity (I); and Book Λ (Lambda), the theology: the unmoved mover, pure actuality, 'thought thinking itself', which moves the cosmos as the object of its love. Books M–N criticise Platonic Forms and numbers.
editions: Ross, Aristotle's Metaphysics, 2 vols. with commentary (1924); Jaeger, OCT (1957)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Clarendon volumes (Bostock on Z/H, 1994; Kirwan on Γ/Δ/E, 1971)

works.title: Nicomachean Ethics

date.note: Named for Aristotle's son (or father) Nicomachus, probably as dedicatee or editor.

works.extent: Complete, 10 books; Books V–VII are shared with the Eudemian Ethics ('the common books'). Bekker 1094a–1181b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; the most influential ethical work in Western history.
works.authenticity: Genuine. The relation to the Eudemian Ethics and the ownership of the three common books is a live scholarly question (Kenny argued the common books are originally Eudemian).
works.summary: Eudaimonia (flourishing) as the human good — 'activity of the soul in accordance with virtue' over a complete life; virtue of character as a mean between excess and deficiency, disposed by habituation; the voluntary, choice, and responsibility; the particular virtues (courage, temperance, justice…); practical wisdom (phronēsis); weakness of will (akrasia); pleasure; friendship (philia, two whole books); and the closing elevation of the contemplative life (theōria) as the highest happiness. The founding text of virtue ethics.
editions: Bywater, Aristotelis Ethica Nicomachea (OCT, 1894)
translations: Ross (rev. Brown, Oxford World's Classics); Irwin (Hackett, 2nd ed. 1999); Broadie & Rowe (2002); Crisp (Cambridge, 2000)

works.title: Eudemian Ethics

date.note: Generally thought the earlier of the two Ethics; named for Eudemus of Rhodes.

works.extent: Extant in 8 books, three of which (IV–VI) are the books shared with the Nicomachean Ethics (= NE V–VII). Bekker 1214a–1249b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; long neglected in favour of the Nicomachean, but increasingly studied on its own terms.
works.authenticity: Genuine. Its independent value and its relation to the NE are actively debated.
works.summary: A parallel treatment of eudaimonia and virtue, sharing the doctrine of the mean and practical wisdom but with distinctive discussions — notably the virtue of kalokagathia ('nobility-and-goodness') in the final book, and a different account of the relation of the virtues to fortune and to god.
editions: Walzer & Mingay, Aristotelis Ethica Eudemia (OCT, 1991)
translations: Inwood & Woolf (Cambridge, 2013); Kenny (Oxford, 2011); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Magna Moralia (Great Ethics)
works.extent: Complete, 2 books. Bekker 1181a–1213b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Disputed. Either an early work of Aristotle, a students' redaction of his lectures, or (the common view) a work by an early Peripatetic. Its Greek is un-Aristotelian, but some (Cooper) have defended a genuine core.
works.summary: A more elementary and schematic ethics covering the same ground as the other two treatises — the good, virtue, the mean, responsibility, friendship — of interest partly for what it shows about how the school digested Aristotle's ethics.
editions: Susemihl, Teubner (1883); Bekker text
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984); Stock (Oxford, 1915, public domain)

works.title: Politics
works.extent: Complete, 8 books (the intended order of the books is disputed). Bekker 1252a–1342b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; conceived as the sequel to the Ethics (the two form a single inquiry into the human good, individual then collective).
works.authenticity: Genuine; possibly assembled from separately composed treatises, hence the debate over book order (the 'Jaeger question').
works.summary: Man as by nature a political animal (zōon politikon); the household, slavery, property, and the critique of Plato's Republic (Bk II); citizenship and the classification of constitutions — the six-fold scheme of correct (kingship, aristocracy, polity) and deviant (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy) forms; the causes of revolution and constitutional stability; and the sketch of the best state and its education (Bks VII–VIII). The foundational work of political science.
editions: Ross, Aristotelis Politica (OCT, 1957); Dreizehnter (1970)
translations: Reeve (Hackett, 1998; 2nd ed. 2017); Barker/Stalley (Oxford); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Constitution of the Athenians (Athēnaiōn Politeia)
works.genre: constitutional history (the sole survivor of the 158 Constitutions)
works.extent: Nearly complete — the beginning is lost. NOT in Bekker (recovered later); cited by chapter/section.
works.transmission: Unique: unknown through the medieval corpus, it was recovered on papyrus rolls acquired by the British Museum and published by F.G. Kenyon in 1891 — the most spectacular Aristotelian find of modern times. (Fragments had also turned up on a Berlin papyrus in 1880.)
works.authenticity: Genuine to the school; whether by Aristotle's own hand or a pupil's under his direction is debated, but it is the one surviving specimen of the great collection of 158 constitutions compiled at the Lyceum.
works.summary: Two parts: a history of the Athenian constitution from the earliest times through the reforms of Solon, the tyranny of Peisistratus, Cleisthenes, and the 5th-century democracy; then a systematic description of the democratic institutions of Aristotle's own day — the Council, the assembly, the magistracies, the law-courts, the allotment machines. Our single most important source for how Athenian democracy actually worked.
editions: Kenyon, Aristotle on the Constitution of Athens (1891); Chambers, Teubner (1986)
translations: Rhodes, Aristotle: The Athenian Constitution (Penguin, 1984); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)
works.notes: Teaching point: the one Constitution that survived did so by accident of the Egyptian sand, not by the manuscript tradition — a vivid lesson in how much of antiquity's loss is contingent.

works.title: Rhetoric (Art of Rhetoric)
works.extent: Complete, 3 books. Bekker 1354a–1420b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus.
works.authenticity: Genuine.
works.summary: Rhetoric as the 'counterpart of dialectic', the faculty of observing the available means of persuasion: the three modes of proof — ethos (character), pathos (emotion), logos (argument, via the enthymeme and example); the three genres (deliberative, forensic, epideictic); a systematic analysis of the emotions (the earliest we have); and Book III on style and arrangement. Foundational for rhetoric and, via the treatment of the passions, for moral psychology.
editions: Ross, Aristotelis Ars Rhetorica (OCT, 1959); Kassel (1976)
translations: Kennedy, Aristotle on Rhetoric (1991; 2nd ed. 2007); Revised Oxford Translation (1984)

works.title: Poetics
works.extent: Only the first book survives (on tragedy and epic); the second book, on comedy, is lost. Bekker 1447a–1462b.
works.transmission: Andronican corpus; recovered for the West largely via the Latin translation of William of Moerbeke and the Arabic tradition. The lost Book II on comedy is the celebrated absence at the heart of Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose.
works.authenticity: Genuine; extant text is the first book only, and even that is compressed and possibly a working draft.
works.summary: The theory of poetry as mimesis (imitation): the definition of tragedy; its six parts (plot, character, thought, diction, spectacle, song), with plot (mythos) primary; the reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnōrisis); the tragic hero and hamartia; and catharsis — the purgation or clarification of pity and fear, defined in a single much-argued phrase. The most influential work of literary criticism ever written.
editions: Kassel, Aristotelis De Arte Poetica (OCT, 1965); Tarán & Gutas (2012)
translations: Halliwell (Loeb, 1995); Janko (Hackett, 1987, with a conjectural reconstruction of Book II); Heath (Penguin, 1996)

works.title: Works spuriously transmitted in the corpus (De Mundo, Economics, Problems, Mechanics, Rhetoric to Alexander, MXG, etc.)
works.extent: A cluster of works carried under Aristotle's name in the Bekker edition but not by him.
citations: Bekker pages within the corpus (e.g. De Mundo 391a–401b; Problems 859a–967b; Mechanics 847a–858b)
works.transmission: Attached to the corpus in antiquity and printed by Bekker, later filtered out by scholarship.
works.authenticity: Spurious (Peripatetic or later). Includes: On the Universe (De Mundo, probably 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE); Economics (Oeconomica, partly Peripatetic, Bk III surviving only in Latin); On Virtues and Vices; the Problems (Problemata, a genuine Peripatetic accretion around a possibly Aristotelian core); Mechanics; On Colours; On Things Heard; Physiognomonics; On Plants (via Arabic, by Nicolaus of Damascus); On Marvellous Things Heard; On Indivisible Lines; Situations and Names of Winds; On Melissus, Xenophanes, and Gorgias (MXG, our source for Gorgias' On Not-Being); and the Rhetoric to Alexander (by Anaximenes of Lampsacus).
works.summary: Doxographically and historically valuable despite the false ascription — the MXG preserves Presocratic material, De Mundo is a key Stoicising cosmological synthesis, the Problems a huge miscellany of scientific questions, and Rhetoric to Alexander the only other surviving 4th-century rhetorical handbook.
editions: Bekker (1831); individual Loeb and Budé editions
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984), which includes several under 'dubia'
works.notes: Rhetoric to Alexander should be cross-linked to Anaximenes of Lampsacus; MXG to Gorgias.

works.title: The lost exoteric works (dialogues: Eudemus, Protrepticus, On Philosophy, On the Good, On Ideas, Gryllus)

date.note: Mostly earlier, some from Aristotle's Academy years.

works.extent: Lost; survive only in fragments and testimonia (Rose³, Ross's Select Fragments). These were the works Aristotle published and by which antiquity knew him.
citations: Rose³ (1886); Ross, Aristotelis Fragmenta Selecta (OCT, 1955); Cicero, various; Iamblichus, Protrepticus
works.transmission: Quoted by Cicero (who read them), Plutarch, Proclus, Iamblichus, and others. Iamblichus' own Protrepticus incorporates long stretches of Aristotle's, allowing partial reconstruction; Cicero modelled works on the Aristotelian dialogues and preserves the 'golden river' judgement.
works.authenticity: Genuine but lost. Reconstructing them (esp. On Philosophy and the Protrepticus) was central to Werner Jaeger's developmental thesis (1923) that Aristotle began a Platonist and evolved away from the Forms.
works.summary: Eudemus, or On the Soul — a dialogue for a dead friend arguing (Platonically) for the soul's immortality and pre-existence. Protrepticus — an exhortation to the philosophical life, hugely influential. On Philosophy — a three-book work with the history of wisdom, a critique of the Forms, and an argument for god from the order of the heavens (the source of the 'argument from design' and of the idea that religion arose from dreams and astronomy). On the Good and On the Ideas — reporting and criticising Plato's unwritten doctrines (our best evidence for them). Gryllus — an early dialogue on rhetoric against Isocrates.
editions: Rose, Aristotelis qui ferebantur librorum fragmenta³ (1886); Ross, Select Fragments (1955); Gigon (1987)
translations: Barnes (ed.), Revised Oxford Translation (1984), vol. 2, 'Fragments'; Hutchinson & Johnson's reconstruction of the Protrepticus (ongoing)
works.notes: The great irony to teach: the polished works Aristotle meant for the public are gone; the private lecture-notes he never meant to publish are the corpus. Our 'Aristotle' is his filing cabinet.

works.title: The lost research corpus (158 Constitutions, Homeric Problems, records, letters, poems)
works.extent: Lost apart from the Athenian Constitution (see above) and scattered fragments. Ancient catalogues (Diogenes Laertius V.22–27, listing ~150 titles in ~400 'books'; the Hesychian and Ptolemaic lists) record a research output several times the size of the surviving corpus.
works.transmission: Known from the ancient book-lists and from quotations. The Constitutions were excerpted by Heraclides Lembus; the Homeric Problems by later scholiasts; the Didascaliae (records of dramatic productions) underlie later theatrical chronology.
works.authenticity: Genuine Lyceum output, much of it collaborative research.
works.summary: The 158 (or 170+) Constitutions of Greek and barbarian states — the empirical base of the Politics; the Didascaliae and Victories at the Dionysia (theatre history); the Homeric Problems (literary criticism); the Customs of the Barbarians; the Pythionikai (Pythian victor-lists, jointly with Callisthenes); the collections of natural-scientific observations; the Letters; and a handful of poems (the Hymn to Virtue for Hermias survives in fragments).
editions: Rose³ (1886); Gigon (1987); Constitutions in Heraclides Lembus, ed. Dilts (1971)
translations: Revised Oxford Translation (1984), 'Fragments'
works.notes: The scale — perhaps a million words of research now lost — is the measure of the Lyceum as the first research institution.

works.title: Ancient catalogues and biography (DL V; the corpus's transmission)
works.extent: The Lives and the three ancient catalogues of Aristotle's works, plus the transmission story.
citations: the anonymous Vita Menagiana and the Vita Marciana
works.transmission: Diogenes Laertius preserves the fullest ancient catalogue. Strabo and Plutarch tell the story of the manuscripts' descent to Neleus and their rediscovery, and of Andronicus of Rhodes' edition (c. 60 BCE) that created the corpus as we have it.
works.authenticity: Not by Aristotle; the framework of the corpus. The Andronicus story is itself debated — some scholars think the treatises circulated more continuously than the romantic cellar-tale implies.
works.summary: The biography (Stagira, twenty years in Plato's Academy, tutor to Alexander, the Lyceum, flight to Chalcis 'lest Athens sin twice against philosophy', death 322 BCE); the catalogues; and the editorial history that determined which Aristotle survived.
editions: Diogenes Laertius, ed. Dorandi (2013); Düring, Aristotle in the Ancient Biographical Tradition (1957)
translations: Hicks, Diogenes Laertius, Loeb (1925) — public domain

excluded.title: Rhetoric to Alexander (Rhetorica ad Alexandrum)
excluded.reason: Transmitted in the corpus and printed by Bekker (1420b–1447b) but by Anaximenes of Lampsacus; the earliest surviving Greek rhetorical handbook.

excluded.title: On Plants (De Plantis)
excluded.reason: The Greek is a retranslation from Arabic and Latin; the work is by Nicolaus of Damascus, a Peripatetic of the age of Augustus.

excluded.title: Secretum Secretorum (Secret of Secrets)
excluded.reason: A hugely popular medieval 'letter of Aristotle to Alexander' on statecraft and health, translated from Arabic; entirely pseudonymous.

excluded.title: Liber de Causis
excluded.reason: Circulated in the Latin Middle Ages as Aristotle's; Aquinas himself identified it as excerpts from Proclus' Elements of Theology.

sources: Bekker, Aristotelis Opera (Berlin, 1831) — the citation base
Barnes (ed.), The Complete Works of Aristotle: Revised Oxford Translation (1984)
Rose, Aristotelis qui ferebantur librorum fragmenta³ (1886); Ross, Select Fragments (1955)
Düring, Aristotle in the Ancient Biographical Tradition (1957)
